new_statements.relation_note: The catalog final stress is fixed final stress; Kaufman & Himmelmann place Besemah in the final-prominence group. Compatible, with the caveat that the chapter does not decide whether the final prominence is word stress or phrase-level prominence, and the evidence is a citation of an unpublished acoustic study (McDonnell 2014), not a description of their own.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Besemah is listed among the Sumatran languages with final-syllable prominence, i.e. the chapter's 'Western Rim prototype' (prominence on the last syllable, at the word or phrase level). The statement is second-hand: the authors cite McDonnell 2014, 'Acoustic correlates of stress in Besemah', an unpublished University of Hawai'i manuscript, and explicitly decline to say anything further about Western Rim languages.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Besemah. The chapter notes only that in the Western Rim prototype final prominence may be word-level or phrase-level, and that 'exceptions abound' in the region (Nias, Mentawai, Batak have penultimate prominence).
new_statements.identity_note: Kaufman & Himmelmann refer to 'Besemah' without dialect qualification, via McDonnell 2014 (a University of Hawai'i manuscript; McDonnell's fieldwork is on Besemah of the Pagar Alam area, South Sumatra, though the chapter does not say so). Helfrich 1904 describes the 'Midden-Maleisch' of the afdeeling Manna and Pasemah Ulu Manna, Residentie Bengkulu, distinguishing a Besemah (B) and a Serawai (S) dialect; his stress statement is given jointly for both.

readall_conflicts: The one listed work (Kaufman & Himmelmann 2024, draft p. 3) agrees with the catalog's final stress, citing McDonnell 2014. A second source already held by the project in the same folder but not in the READALL works list disagrees: Helfrich, O. L. 1904, Bijdragen tot de kennis van het Midden-Maleisch (Besemahsch en Serawajsch dialect), Verhandelingen van het Bataviaasch Genootschap 53, section 'Klemtoon', printed pp. 200-201 (pp. 222-223; file, line 25668): "De klemtoon is in tegenstelling met die in het Maleisch vrij sterk en valt op de voorlaatste lettergreep, zelfs in afgeleide woorden, welke door een aanhechtsel langer zijn geworden dan het stamwoord. Heeft echter de voorlaatste lettergreep de doffe »ë" en is die niet gesloten dan valt de klemtoon op de laatste lettergreep" (translation: "The stress, in contrast to that of Malay, is fairly strong and falls on the penultimate syllable, even in derived words which have become longer than the stem through an affix. If however the penultimate syllable has the dull ë [schwa] and is not closed, then the stress falls on the last syllable"). Helfrich's 1904 impressionistic account thus gives penultimate stress with schwa-conditioned shift to the ultima (the classic Malay pattern), for both the Besemah (B) and Serawai (S) dialects he describes, which contradicts the catalog's fixed: final syllable reading and Kaufman & Himmelmann's placement of Besemah in the final-prominence group. Glottolog's 15 descriptive refs for cent2053 are Helfrich's 1904-1933 Dutch materials and Indonesian morphology/syntax sketches of the various South Barisan lects; none is a better stress source, and web search found no JIPA Illustration or later prosodic study. sources.note: This work describes Benakat (dialek o), spoken in seven villages along the Benakat river, Kecamatan Gunung Megang and Kecamatan Talang Ubi, Kabupaten Muara Enim, South Sumatra; the book never mentions Besemah/Pasemah. Word-level prosody (pitch, stress, tempo, juncture) is stated to be non-functional, i.e. non-contrastive; prosody only operates at sentence level as declarative vs interrogative intonation. No stress position is given, no secondary stress, no weight, no length; so nothing bears on the catalog's final-stress rule (McDonnell 2016, from Besemah). Consistent with the catalog's no-to…
